Sally: Jennifer Andrews, you are a biology teacher and an activist involved in the preservation of the Amazonian Rainforest. What was the factor that started it all?
Jennifer Andrews: I read so much about it. I've always dreamed of sailing down the Amazon River and being surrounded by the rainforest. I wanted to experience the emotions that explorers felt as they walked through the thick foliage for the first time.

Sally: Were you inspired by the writings of the scientists who explored the forest before you?
Jennifer Andrews: Absolutely. The first book about the rainforest was written in 1542 by a Spanish explorer. This is the book which I found most inspiring.

Sally: What made you decide to become an activist?
Jennifer Andrews: As I was surfing around the Internet, I stumbled upon many websites that advocate rainforest conservation. I found out that many species were threatened by human activity. What I didn't realize was that the companies that are cutting down the trees for the logging industry might completely destroy the forest by the year 2030. The rainforest was created by nature to clean the air that we breathe.

When you are writing a news article or giving an interview, you can include the Simple Past Passive to describe something done by someone at sometime in the past.
In a regular sentence structure, you use Subject + verb + object.

Example:
A Spanish explorer wrote the first book about the rainforest.
In the Simple Past Passive form, you use the structure:
Object + was / were + past participle + by Subject

Example:
The first book about the rainforest was written in 1542 by a Spanish explorer.
You can use the Simple Past Passive to ask questions:
Was / Were + Object + past participle + by Subject

Example:
Were you inspired by the writings of the scientists who explored the forest before you?

When you want to clarify which person or thing you are talking about, you use a relative clause.

You can begin a relative clause with who for people, which for things or that for either people or things.

In spoken English you usually use that, rather than which or who.

You put the relative clause immediately after the noun it talks about.
A subject relative clause describes the subject of the clause.

Example:
The man who called wanted to speak to Tom.
Which man? The man who called.
The clause who called immediately follows man - the noun it describes.
An object relative clause describes the object of the clause.

Example:
Can you return the book that I lent you?
Which book? The book I lent you.
